items.title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
items.content: <article>The mammoth figure surpasses every video game launch and single-day film box office record.</article>
items.lbText:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have become the biggest entertainment launch in history following the blockbuster video game's debut on Thursday , after a 13-year wait.

The highly anticipated open-world action-adventure saw pre-orders and first day sales total more than 24.5 million units, raking in about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics platform Sensor Tower.

In comparison, this year's highest grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas .

GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both the firms for comment.

The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history .

At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.

The latest release follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.

GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop , which would make it the most expensive video game in history.

Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.

The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.

Around three quarters of the game's sales have been for the PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.

Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.

That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind , which has made an estimated $4.5bn, adjusted for inflation.

Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.

The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.

If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.

Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grown through repeated delays, following a 13-year wait.

GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece.

The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play.

Its launch broke Virgin Media O2's evening traffic record as people rushed to install GTA 6's huge 212GB file on consoles.

The game's graphic content has resulted in censorship in Japan and, like earlier GTA releases, is not approved for sale in mainland China.

items.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
items.content: <article>Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.</article>
items.lbText:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.

The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets, with the S&P 500 down more than 2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.7% by lunchtime.

Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 3.4% by the middle of trading on Friday.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 12% to about $85 by lunchtime, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.

The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.

The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell.

Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.

Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - were also trading lower. Germany's Dax index fell 2% and the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

items.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
items.content: <article>The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.</article>
items.lbText:
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

items.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
items.content: <article>The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.</article>
items.lbText:
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.

Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.

There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."

On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.

Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".

The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.

Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."

The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.

Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.

"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.

Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".

Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".

Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

items.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
items.content: <article>The trade deal is unlikely lower food prices for shoppers, but should boost the economy more than other post-Brexit agreements.</article>
items.lbText:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

items.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
items.content: <article>New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do could mean fewer chores but higher costs for customers.</article>
items.lbText:
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.

Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.

Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".

But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.

The new Airbnb rules, announced last month , allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.

Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts , external "who need to take action" it said.

Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.

If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.

But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.

Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party.

There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.

Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.

She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.

The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.

She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.

"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said.

The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year.

Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.

Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however.

Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably.

items.title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
items.content: <article>People stocking up on long-life food drove retail sales higher October, according to official data.</article>
items.lbText:
Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures , external .

Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying .

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

"Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said:

"Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again."

The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the uptick came after a 0.6% decline in September.

As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October.

The boost in sales comes at the beginning of the festive period, which is normally the busiest time of the year for retailers.

Jacqui Baker, partner and head of retail at auditing firm RSM UK, said that "retailers will want to see out the year with some Christmas cheer before consumers batten down the hatches in the New Year as energy costs skyrocket and inflation ramps up further".

Typical energy bills are forecast to go up by £443 per year from January, pushing up the pace of price rises.

Separate economic data released on Friday showed the government borrowed slightly less than economists had expected in October.

Borrowing - the difference between public sector spending and income - was £17bn last month, the ONS said. , external

Although that was £0.8bn higher than October last year, it was below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn.

Interest repayments were £11.2bn - the highest October debt interest figure on record - and £2.8bn more than a year ago.

These repayments have been pushed up by higher inflation, as payments on index-linked government bonds are linked to the inflation rate.

Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices. The rate has been rising in recent months as the Iran war has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

items.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
items.content: <article>Would AI be a good judge of whether you should get a mortgage, car loan or mobile phone contract?</article>
items.lbText:
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.

It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.

"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.

Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.

"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.

Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.

"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.

"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.

Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.

But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?

In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.

But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".

But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.

"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.

Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".

While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.

She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.

"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.

Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score.

"I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a £30-a-month phone contract, and they said no," she recalls.

"When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the big three credit reference agencies."

That experience inspired her to try to change the system.

In 2021, Atkinson founded a credit reference agency with her best-friend from school, who had also experienced difficulties getting credit.

Their firm, Noggin HQ, was authorised by the FCA in June. Atkinson explains it was set up to help consumers access affordable credit by analysing their current account transactional data.

The platform helps lenders interpret thousands of individual data points about a person's spending habits.

Crucially, it does this without using AI, which Atkinson has also argued "carries the risk of inbuilt bias".

"You have to be very careful", she warns. "It's very sensitive data and it would be very easy for the models to be inferring various kind of protected characteristics."

Perhaps conscious of change, the big three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting users check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax launched a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it says uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.

Meanwhile, in March TransUnion announced it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".…

items.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
items.content: <article>Would AI be a good judge of whether you should get a mortgage, car loan or mobile phone contract?</article>
items.lbText:
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.

It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.

"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.

items.title: Social poker with £5 stake is booming, says dealer
items.content: <article>A poker league in Fenland sees a 35% rise in players since 2022.</article>
items.lbText:
A man who organises social poker sessions in pubs and clubs said the game's growing popularity could be down to the cost-of-living crisis.

Phillip Steer, from March, Cambridgeshire, has run poker nights in Fenland for 14 years and said he has seen a 35% rise in the number of players in the area since 2022, with now about "100 players across 15 clubs and pubs".

Steer added that as people can only place a maximum £5 stake, the game was often "cheaper" than other pastimes.

Player Violet Cunningham said: "I have been playing poker for about 10 years; it's nice to get out of the house... it's fun and exciting."

Tom Brady, the director of Live Pub Poker League (LPPL), said he had also seen an increase in the number of players joining for social tournaments in pubs and venues post-Covid, with the past 12 months being particularly busy.

On a chilly November evening about 15 people congregated in a pub in March, where they are given the use of a warm side room to set up their poker tables, cards and chips.

Steer said all sorts of people get involved in the game, adding: "We have men, women, retired and working people."

He said most people treat the game as a bit of fun and he did not worry that players would get into debt by taking part, due to the low-value stake.

"You buy 12,000 chips at the start of the night for £5 and once those have gone it is game over," he added.

Donald Rofe is a widower and lives alone in March, he said his family live in Wisbech and Cambridge.

"[Poker] gets me out of the house, although I have recently had my cataracts done, so I have some issues with reading the cards properly," he said.

Rofe admitted that he mistook a diamond for a heart, which cost him a victory.

"I put in all my chips because I thought I had a flush but I didn't, but it was still fun", he added.

The cost of play is another bonus for Rofe, who added he normally has one soft drink that will "last me all night".

Violet Cunningham is a full-time carer and said she liked to relax by playing poker.

"I have been playing poker for about 10 years, it's nice to get out of the house - it makes your brain tick, it's fun and exciting, but can be frustrating," she said.

Cunningham said she and her family grew up playing card games on holiday and she has always enjoyed playing them.

"I think women are harder to read than the men, play a bit tighter, unless they have it [a good hand] they probably won't bet on it," she added.

The Gambling Commission , external said that pub poker was classed as "exempt gaming" and can be carried out without a gambling licence or permit.

Players cannot place a stake more than £5 and combined stakes for the premises hosting the game cannot exceed £100 per day.

items.title: Survey reveals 'major increase' in cost of living
items.content: <article>More than two thirds of respondents reported noticing rises in the cost of living.</article>
items.lbText:
There has been "a major increase" in the overall cost of living in the past 12 months in Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man, a survey has found.

Island Global Research, a market research and consultancy company, found more than 69% of respondents in Jersey, 68% in Guernsey and 70% in the Isle of Man said they had noticed a cost increase , external .

The survey, which was completed by over 1,000 people in each island, saw 57% of respondents describe themselves as "less than comfortable" with about one in 10 going without essentials like food and heating.

The survey also found 65% said they now spent less on non essentials and 53% said they are shopping around more because of the price rises.

In Jersey, 10% of respondents reported they could not afford the increased costs and often have to go with out essentials, while in Guernsey it was 11%.

The survey also showed that two thirds of people in Jersey said they had found it difficult to meet living costs in the last 12 months, an increase of 17 percentage points compared to 2024 .

Guernsey also saw an increase with 58% reporting they found it difficult to meet living costs.

The survey also found about one in four received support to help finance their everyday living expenses in the last six months.

On the Isle of Man, 36% said they cut back on groceries and 30% received support to help finance everyday living expenses over a six-month period.

items.title: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad
items.content: <article>The properties are marketed at premium prices with claims of “government-backed” returns, the BBC finds.</article>
items.lbText:
"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.

But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.

The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.

A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.

The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.

About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.

The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.

Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.

While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support .

Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment.

We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.

Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".

The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.

Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.

Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.

Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.

Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently.

Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common.

The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan.

But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act.

He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat.

"Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building."

Phil had no idea the flat he rents had been sold to overseas investors in May 2025 until the BBC contacted him. But there were clues: bills addressed to someone called Jan Hála had been coming through the letterbox for months.

Lee Jones told us that the properties his companies provide are "good quality accommodation" and he has no responsibility for the communal areas of Castleview House since he sold the freehold in 2021. He denied his relationship with Chris Smith amounted to a conflict of interest, but did not respond to questions about his role in marketing the properties.

Jan Hála, the Czech investor who now owns Phil's flat, and the Britské Reality estate agency did not respond to requests for comment.

We spoke to several other people living in flats run by Nurture Housing Association in Castleview House who said they were in supported accommodation. They reported receiving little or no help from Nurture but were afraid to speak out publicly for fear of eviction and becoming homeless.

There is also evidence that marketing materials for investors buying flats in Castleview were misleading. Investors were told Nurture was providing "specialist supported housing" - a claim which is repeated on its website.…

items.title: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work
items.content: <article>Eating at your desk? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work</article>
items.lbText:
There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's.

Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish.

From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive.

"We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah.

She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left".

Casey, a content creator for an energy company, says he used to eat tuna at his desk but has since "reformed".

He says you have to "suss out the smelliness" and then decide if it's acceptable to eat at the desk.

But fish isn't the only food causing office friction and Casey says his regular snack of cinnamon pretzels has been causing "quite a bit of havoc".

"The sugar's going everywhere and it's getting in my laptop keys," he admits. No-one in the office has commented on it yet but he says he's hiding the crumbs by "shuffling them off the desk".

Boiled eggs also split opinion. Laura, who works in finance, says she's been teased by colleagues for eating them.

"In my defence, it was high protein, it was cost-effective and healthy – I swear by a good boiled egg."

She thinks that no food is off limits at the desk. "Coming from an Asian background where you'd eat fish for breakfast I am very open to it being eaten."

Ashlea Fisher, who runs her own recruitment company, has tackled the issue of smelly food in the office head on when she asked a member of staff to stop bringing in fish after "the smell was so bad that a pregnant colleague was feeling physically sick".

"I'm a big believer in being able to have an honest conversation with your team," she says, and suggests that other people in her position should approach a conversation lightly and be conscious of not embarrassing colleagues.

"Nobody should feel judged for what they eat, and we should respect different cultures and dietary requirements, but being mindful of the people around you is simply good workplace etiquette."

While what we eat in the office at lunch can cause tension, there's also the question of whether we're even taking the time to enjoy our lunch in the first place.

In a world of back-to-back meetings and overflowing inboxes, it's easy to skip our break and shovel down a sandwich with one hand while replying to emails with the other.

A 2025 report by Just Eat found that the youngest workers, Gen Z, were the most likely to take a full break, with 56% doing so.

However, the next generation up, millennials were more likely than any other to eat lunch at their desk.

"While it can be convenient to eat at your desk, it's not best practice to remain glued to the screen all day," says Alan Price, an employment law and HR expert, and CEO of BrightHR.

"Taking a break isn't just an employment right, there are proven benefits for both physical and mental health."

Laura, whose working day can occasionally finish at 2am, says stepping away from her desk is a non-negotiable and she makes a point of taking an hour for lunch, describing it as "essential for maintaining my sanity".

"I take my lunch break as much as possible, for the sake of my eyes and mental wellbeing," she says.

But others are less precious about it. Content creator Manny says he has lunch at his desk "most of the time".

His work is task-based and his company operates a policy of "do the work when you want to do it".

"Usually you just take 20 minutes to eat something, but on another day you might take an hour. You just kind of feel it out," he says.

items.title: Tens of thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret nationwide operation
items.content: <article>Supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants and stadiums have been scrambling to make their devices safe.</article>
items.lbText:
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.

Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.

France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies .

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.

In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.

The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.

The security threat was discovered by ethical hackers at a firm called Omega Systems - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pentest Partners who helped raise the alarm.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.

They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.

Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely, or in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.

BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.

"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did want to be publicly named.

"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.

There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:

In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted

On 11th and 12th October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted

On the 1st and 2nd of November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium, Luxembourg the were worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted

The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).

RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.

As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.

These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.

"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.

"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.

RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.

The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.

"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.

He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included, dismantling our hardware".

"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.

RDM confirmed that there is no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continues to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.

items.title: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
items.content: <article>The BBC's Samira Hussain breaks down the AI company's first day as a publicly traded company, as shares closed up 17%.</article>
items.lbText:
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, closed 17% higher on its first day as a publicly traded company. Shares closed at $97.17, giving the company a market valuation of around $1.77 trillion, after briefly surpassing $2 trillion during trading.

The debut came as the wider technology sector fell 2.4%, raising questions about investor confidence in the AI boom.

The BBC's Samira Hussain breaks down Anthropic's first day on the stock market.

items.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
items.content: <article>Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.</article>
items.lbText:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each , showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.

The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate more quickly tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet.

It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.

The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.

That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.

Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.

Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.

But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.

"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.

Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.

"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."

A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."

The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.

Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.

Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".

Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut

items.title: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
items.content: <article>The probe by California, where the AI chipmaker has its global headquarters, follows former CEO Jensen Huang's departure. </article>
items.lbText:
California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.

"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.

Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.

Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.

Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.

Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.

Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

items.title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
items.content: <article>The company behind the Claude chatbot will become one of the most valuable firms in the world.</article>
items.lbText:
Anthropic is poised to hit a value of more than $1.4 trillion (£1.1 trillion) when it debuts on the public stock market.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said it will price shares at $83 each when it lists on Thursday on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.

That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.

It will be the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge investment poured into the technology will be profitable.

The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.

But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.

The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.

If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.

Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.

However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price .

As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.

The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June .

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.

Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.

The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires

There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.

Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.

While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.

"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads investment strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.

Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders , led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.

The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.

It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way. And Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.

Nonetheless, the company is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.

Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."

But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.

The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.

A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".

items.title: Viagogo may have broken law on hidden fees, watchdog provisionally finds
items.content: <article>The UK's competition body says initial findings suggest the ticket-reselling website used drip pricing.</article>
items.lbText:
Ticket-reselling site Viagogo may have broken the law on hidden fees, the UK's competition body has said in a provisional finding.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it found that Viagogo failed to show consumers the total price upfront when they were buying tickets "and added fees later in the process, a practice known as drip pricing".

The CMA added that this was an initial finding, and it should not be assumed that the company had actually broken the law.

In a statement, Viagogo said it was co-operating fully with the CMA, adding that the investigation was continuing and "no final findings have been made".

The CMA said last year that it was investigating a number of companies over their online pricing practices, including Viagogo.

The competition watchdog said it had looked into the experience of UK fans buying tickets for events such as concerts and sport on three websites that operate under the Viagogo brand.

"The CMA believes that mandatory costs such as taxes and booking fees were added at later stages of the checkout process and not included in the total price from the start," it said.

"Drip pricing can cause fans to be caught out by extra charges and buy tickets they might not otherwise have selected, had they been able to compare prices accurately from the start."

The CMA said Viagogo would now have an opportunity to consider its findings and respond before a final decision is made.

"This is an ongoing investigation and no final findings have been made," Viagogo said in a statement.

"We have engaged constructively with the CMA and continue to cooperate fully with its investigation."

The CMA has powers to tackle anti-competitive behaviour. It can now decide if consumer laws have been broken - rather than having to go through the courts.

Drip pricing is one of the practices the CMA has been focusing on particularly.

On Wednesday, it said it was investigating three companies , external over the issue, and in August it announced that the Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and RED Driving School had been engaged in the practice.

In general, the CMA can impose penalties of up to 10% of global turnover for a breach of consumer law. However, it will consider a number of factors, including the severity of conduct, before deciding on the size of the penalty.

In June this year, the watchdog ordered rival ticket reseller StubHub UK to refund more than 50,000 customers and pay a £900,000 fine for not showing people the total price upfront when buying tickets.

StubHub UK received a 40% reduction to its financial penalty after it admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early with the CMA.

items.title: Gilts v kilts: What is happening with Scottish government bonds?
items.content: <article>MSPs have heard both the pros and cons of the government's plan to launch its first ever bond to the market.</article>
items.lbText:
The Scottish government is facing questions about its plan to issue its first ever bonds.

The move would allow ministers to borrow money from investors who in return receive regular interest payments.

The aim is to raise about £1.5bn by the end of the parliamentary term, with the funds to be used on long-term projects such as building hospitals or maintaining roads.

Named "kilts", a nod to UK government "gilts", the scheme has provoked much debate.

This week, MSPs on Holyrood's finance committee heard about the potential risks and rewards.

A bond is a financial tool used by a government to borrow money. They are sold with a promise for the buyer, or investor, to be paid back at the end of an agreed term.

The government will also make regular payments to the investor.

In the UK, a government bond is called a gilt. They are typically bought by financial institutions such as pension funds, insurance companies and commercial banks.

As a play on this term, the Scottish bonds have been nicknamed "kilts".

The Scottish government has said it expects the bonds to be issued within this financial year, subject to market conditions.

Former First Minister Humza Yousaf commissioned initial work in 2023 after advisers in the Scottish government's Investor Panel recommended making bonds available to the market as a means of raising Scotland's profile and attracting investment.

In November last year, the government announced that it had received an identical credit rating to the UK's score.

This was based on "prudent fiscal management" and the country's economic stability - though ministers were warned this could change if Scotland moved towards independence.

With market volatility due to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, some have questioned whether now is a good time to launch bonds.

But at Holyrood, David McMillan, professor in finance and accounting at the University of Stirling, told MSPs: "You can't wait for a perfect time because there's going to be no perfect time."

The government wants to raise £1.5bn through bonds by 2031, although that would only be a fraction of its near £70bn budget.

About four-fifths of the Scottish government's budget is used on resource spending, which goes towards day-to-day costs such as funding the NHS, benefits payments and paying salaries.

A smaller portion is made up of capital spending, typically used on long-term physical assets such as buildings and bridges, or maintaining roads or paths.

The Scottish government is unable to borrow for resource spending other than to correct forecasting errors.

However, for capital spending, it can borrow as much as £450m a year at 2023-24 levels up to a total cap of £3bn - to be uprated with inflation.

Adjusted for inflation, the government could borrow about £491m in the current financial year, with a total limit of about £3.3bn.

Economists have noted that Scottish bonds would be a more costly way of borrowing than existing routes provided by the UK government through the National Loans Fund.

It has been estimated , external that interest rates on "kilts" would be 0.3 percentage points above gilts, plus an additional £2m per bond in administrative costs.

The Scottish government has not released costings, citing market sensitivities, but has insisted , external issuing bonds would represent value for money relative to the costs of borrowing through the UK scheme.

Ministers argue that issuing bonds would be a good opportunity to market the country to investors, and would be helpful if Scotland became independent.

Dr Ben Cormier, a senior lecturer at the University of Strathclyde's department of government and public policy, told Holyrood's finance committee that while the Scottish bonds could cost marginally more than the UK scheme, they would "bring flexibility to public finances and debt management".

McMillan agreed with the plans "in principle", but warned they would lose "credibility" with investors if limited to five years.

Cormier warned that independence was the one thing "that could materially change the nature of risk associated with Scottish bonds".

Conservative MSP Liam Kerr said bonds could be more expensive than borrowing through the National Loans Fund and voiced concerns about a lack of transparency in the programme.

McMillan agreed there should be "full information" available, saying: "You've got to have a clear, full and frank conversation with the public."
